title: Collision theory
keyIdea: Particles can only react when they collide, and only collisions with at least the activation energy (Ea) are successful. The rate of reaction depends on the frequency of successful collisions. Higher concentration, higher gas pressure and greater surface area give more collisions per second. Higher temperature gives a few more collisions and, more importantly, a much bigger share with energy at least Ea. A catalyst provides a different reaction pathway with a lower activation energy and is not used up.

kid: For a reaction to happen, particles must collide. But most collisions do nothing. The particles just bounce apart. A collision only works if the particles hit with enough energy. The smallest energy needed is the activation energy, Ea. A collision with at least Ea is a successful collision.

The rate of reaction is how fast reactants are used up or products are made. It depends on how many successful collisions happen each second. So there are two ways to speed a reaction up. Make collisions happen more often. Or make a bigger share of them have at least Ea.

Raising the concentration puts more particles in the same space. For a gas, higher pressure does the same thing. Cutting a solid into smaller pieces gives it a larger surface area, so more particles are exposed. All three give more collisions each second. Each collision is no harder than before.

Heating does two things. The particles move faster, so they collide a bit more often. Much more important, a far bigger share of the collisions now have at least Ea. A catalyst gives a different route with a lower Ea. More collisions are then successful. The catalyst is not used up, so it can work again and again.
adult: This lesson covers collision theory and rates of reaction for GCSE Chemistry (AQA 4.6.1.2 to 4.6.1.4, Edexcel 7, OCR Gateway C5.2) and NGSS HS-PS1-5. Key terms are collision frequency, successful collision, activation energy, rate of reaction, concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalyst. The energy graph in the lab is a simple version of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, which is met fully at A level.

The most common mistake is to explain the temperature effect only by more frequent collisions. In the lab, heating from 20 °C to 80 °C raises the hits per second by about a tenth. The successful collisions rise by far more. Ask students to give both reasons, and to say which one matters more. A related misconception is that heating lowers the activation energy. Ea belongs to the reaction route, so only a catalyst changes it.

Students also say that higher concentration makes particles hit harder. Be careful with wording such as more energetic collisions here. Concentration, pressure and surface area change only the frequency of collisions. Another slip is to say that a catalyst gives particles more energy, or that it is used up. Insist on the phrase a different pathway with a lower activation energy.

The model reaction in the lab has a small Ea, so its rate rises more gently with temperature than many real reactions. Each test is the mean of eight runs, which shows why repeat readings matter. A good follow-up is a marble chips and acid practical, timing gas volume with lumps and with powder. Next steps are rate graphs, reaction profiles and, at A level, the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve.

familyTip: Drop half a fizzy vitamin tablet into cold water and the other half into warm water, then a crushed half into cold water. Time each one and ask your learner to explain both results with collision theory, using the words collision frequency and activation energy.

visual.caption: Why does each change speed up the reaction? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

bins: Bigger share of hits reach Ea

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fire particles to see bounces and reactions, then test temperature, concentration and a catalyst in a particle box.

practice.prompt: Which collisions lead to a reaction?
choices: Ones with at least the activation energy
Every collision
Only collisions at the walls
practice.hint: Think about the gentle push that made the particles bounce apart.
practice.explain: Only collisions with energy at least Ea are successful. Most collisions just bounce.

practice.prompt: {n}00 collisions happen each second, and 5% have at least Ea. How many successful collisions happen each second?
practice.hint: Find 5% of the total, which is 5 for every 100.
practice.explain: 5% of {n}00 is 5 × {n} = {=5*n} successful collisions each second.

practice.prompt: Why does powder react faster than a lump of the same solid?
choices: Larger surface area, so more collisions
Powder has a lower activation energy
Powder particles move faster
practice.hint: Which particles of a solid can be hit by acid particles?
practice.explain: Only surface particles can be hit. Powder has far more surface area, so more collisions happen each second.

practice.prompt: A reaction makes {n}0 cm³ of gas in 10 s. What is the mean rate of reaction in cm³ per second?
practice.hint: Mean rate is the amount of product divided by the time taken.
practice.explain: Mean rate = {n}0 cm³ ÷ 10 s = {n} cm³ per second.

practice.prompt: Rate is {n} units. Collision theory says doubling only the acid concentration doubles the collisions. What is the new rate?
practice.hint: Twice the collisions, and the same share of them succeed.
practice.explain: Twice as many collisions each second with the same share succeeding gives 2 × {n} = {=2*n} units.

choices: The least energy a collision needs to react
The energy given out by a reaction
The speed of the fastest particle
pool.hint: Think of the red line on the energy graph in the lab.
pool.explain: Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need for a successful collision.

pool.prompt: Heating a reaction raises its rate. What is the main reason?
choices: A bigger share of collisions have at least Ea
Particles collide a little more often
The activation energy falls
pool.hint: Compare how much the hits and the reactions rose in your test.
pool.explain: Hits rise only a little. The big rise comes from more collisions reaching Ea. Ea itself does not change.

choices: Gives a route with a lower activation energy
Gives the particles more energy
Gets used up as it works
pool.hint: Watch what moved on the energy graph when you turned it on.
pool.explain: A catalyst gives another pathway with a lower Ea and is not used up, so more collisions succeed.

pool.prompt: A rate doubles for every 10 °C rise. At 20 °C the rate is {n}. What is it at 40 °C?
pool.hint: Double once for 30 °C and again for 40 °C.
pool.explain: Two rises of 10 °C double it twice: {n} × 2 × 2 = {=4*n}.

pool.prompt: Higher gas pressure speeds up a gas reaction because…
choices: Particles are closer, so they collide more often
Each collision has more energy
The activation energy is lower
pool.hint: Pressure is like concentration for a gas.
pool.explain: More particles in the same space means more collisions each second. The energy of each one is unchanged.

pool.prompt: {n}00 collisions happen each second. With a catalyst, 20% have at least Ea. How many are successful each second?
pool.explain: 20% of {n}00 is 20 × {n} = {=20*n} successful collisions each second.

pool.prompt: Why does food go off more slowly in a fridge?
choices: Particles move slower, so fewer collisions reach Ea
The cold stops all particles
The cold uses up the catalyst
pool.hint: Particles never stop moving at fridge temperature.
pool.explain: Lower temperature means slower particles: fewer collisions, and far fewer with at least Ea.

pool.prompt: Which change does NOT give more collisions per second?
choices: Adding a catalyst
Raising the concentration
Grinding a solid into powder
pool.hint: One change works on Ea, not on how often particles meet.
pool.explain: A catalyst lowers Ea. Concentration and surface area raise the collision frequency.

pool.prompt: A reaction makes {n} g of product in 20 s. What is its mean rate in g per second? Give it as a decimal.
pool.hint: Divide the mass of product by the time taken.
pool.explain: Mean rate = {n} g ÷ 20 s = {=n/20} g per second.
